prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

[byline] la herradura, s.v.—¿Do I have a mother? Have her pinkie in my hand crossing the street? Have her breath on my hair as she sings arru-rru mi niño to sleep. ¿Don’t you mean where? ¿What was your question? I’m older. Think more about memory. It makes me crazy. Obsessed. Her warm breasts on my belly as she knelt to tell me todo va estar bien. I’ll never see her again was the fear as if she’s gone, died, will never come back. I whispered it hidden in banana groves looking at the sky hoping one of those planes would take me to wherever she had left to. Whenever Mom hung the clothes to dry, not a cloud in the sky. I could see her sandals picking up dust. For a second. For a second I believe she’s back. It went like that every day. Every single night. I’ll never see her again. But then, I did. Her face. Her hair. She was the same. So much had changed. I do not remember what it was I truly felt.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Have, Don, What

outputs.L1: [byline] La Herradura, S.V.—Do I have a mother? Do I have her pinkie in my hand as we cross the street? Her breath on my hair as she sings *arru-rru mi niño* to sleep. Don’t you mean where? What was your question? I’m older now. I think more about memory. It makes me crazy. Obsessed. Her warm breasts against my belly as she knelt to tell me *todo va estar bien*. I’ll never see her again—that was the fear, as if she were gone, dead, never coming back. I whispered it, hidden in the banana groves, looking up at the sky, hoping one of those planes would take me to wherever she had gone. Whenever Mom hung the clothes to dry, there wasn’t a cloud in the sky. I could see her sandals kicking up dust. For a second. For a second, I believed she was back. It went on like that every day. Every single night. I’ll never see her again. But then I did. Her face. Her hair. She was the same. So much had changed. I do not remember what it was I truly felt.
outputs.L2: [byline] la herradura, s.v.—Do I have a mother? Was her little finger wrapped in my palm while we crossed the road? Was her breathing warm against my hair as she lulled me to sleep singing arru-rru mi niño? Don’t you mean where? What were you asking? I am older now. I think about memory more often. It unsettles me. Consumes me. I remember the heat of her breasts against my stomach when she crouched down to tell me todo va estar bien. The terror was: I will never see her again—as though she had vanished, as though she had died, as though she would never return. I murmured those words from where I hid among the banana trees, staring up at the sky, wishing one of the airplanes passing overhead would carry me to whatever place she had gone. Whenever Mom pinned the laundry out to dry, the sky was perfectly clear. I would glimpse her sandals lifting dust from the ground. For one instant. For one instant, I would think she had come back. That was how it happened each day. Every night. I will never see her again. And then I did. Her face. Her hair. She had not changed. Everything else had. I cannot recall what I actually felt.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back on their earliest memories of their mother, but these memories come to them only in fragments. They remember the physical closeness of her presence: the comfort of her body, the feeling of being held, and the sound of lullabies that once soothed them. These details are tender, but they are incomplete, as if the past can only be recovered in small, broken pieces.

Much of the speaker’s reflection is shaped by an intense preoccupation with memory. They seem almost tormented by the effort to understand what happened and to recover what has been lost. The past is not clear or stable; instead, it is something the speaker keeps returning to, trying to make sense of it. This struggle with memory becomes overwhelming, as though the desire to remember fully is driving them nearly mad.

As a child, the speaker feared that their mother had disappeared forever. They did not understand where she had gone, and this absence became frightening and mysterious. In their imagination, airplanes seemed connected to her disappearance. The child imagined that planes might be able to carry them to the unknown place where their mother had gone, offering a possible way to reach her again.

Because the speaker longed so deeply for their mother’s return, ordinary sights in daily life became charged with hope. Clothes drying in the wind or a pair of dusty sandals could briefly make them believe that she had come back. These small, familiar images seemed to contain traces of her presence, and for a moment they blurred the line between memory, hope, and reality.

Eventually, the speaker did see their mother again. However, even this important reunion remains uncertain in memory. The speaker cannot fully recover what they truly felt at that moment. Although the event itself happened, the emotions attached to it are unclear, lost somewhere in the same fragmented past that the speaker has been trying so desperately to understand.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a deeply emotional exploration of childhood memory, centered on the speaker’s experience of maternal absence, fear, and longing. Rather than unfolding as a clear, chronological narrative, the speaker’s recollections appear fragmented, moving through flashes of image, sound, and sensation. These fragments suggest the way trauma is often remembered: not as a complete story, but as scattered impressions that remain vivid even when the exact sequence of events has faded. The use of lyrical language and bilingual expression gives the memories an intimate and personal quality, allowing the reader to feel how closely language, family, and identity are tied to the speaker’s emotional world.

Throughout the text, sensory details from childhood carry much of the emotional weight. Images of rooms, bodies, voices, weather, or domestic spaces become charged with fear and desire, revealing how the speaker experienced the mother’s absence not simply as a fact, but as a physical and emotional condition. The child’s world is shaped by uncertainty: the speaker longs for the mother’s presence while also struggling to understand why she is gone. This uncertainty produces a sense of vulnerability, as the child appears caught between hope and dread, memory and imagination, love and abandonment.

Although the mother eventually returns, her return does not fully heal the wound created by separation. Instead, the text suggests that reunion cannot erase the fear, confusion, or loneliness that marked the speaker’s earlier experience. The mother’s presence may answer one kind of longing, but it does not restore the child’s sense of safety or make the past whole again. In this way, the text resists a simple resolution. It shows that emotional trauma can persist even after the external situation has changed.

Ultimately, the text is less concerned with establishing exactly what happened than with capturing how the speaker remembers and feels what happened. The uncertainty of memory becomes central to the work’s meaning. Events blur, details shift, and the past remains incomplete, but the emotions attached to it endure with striking force. By preserving this instability, the text demonstrates how memory can hold onto fear, longing, and confusion long after the original moment has passed. The mother’s return may bring the story to a kind of conclusion, but it does not bring emotional certainty. Instead, the text reveals how absence continues to live inside memory, shaping the speaker’s understanding of love, loss, and childhood.
outputs.L5:
**Have, Don, What**

Have you ever wondered what makes a person truly kind? Don, a quiet man from a small town, believed that kindness was shown through simple actions. He did not have much money, but he always shared what he could with others.

Every morning, Don would walk to the local bakery and buy an extra loaf of bread. If he saw someone in need, he would offer it with a smile. People often asked, “What makes you do this every day?” Don would simply answer, “If I have something to give, I should give it.”

His words reminded everyone that kindness does not have to be grand or expensive. What matters most is the willingness to help. Don’s small acts made a big difference, and his community became a warmer, more caring place because of him.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical first-person flash memoir in a bilingual Spanish-English voice about childhood separation from a mother, memory, and the fear of never seeing her again, with a byline dateline style opening.
counterfactuals.output:
**By [Name Withheld] — El Paso, Texas, 1999**

The last time I saw my mother that summer, she was standing behind glass, her palm lifted like a small white flag.

I was seven. Or maybe eight. Memory is a house with no straight hallways. In one room, she is wearing her blue blouse, the one with the tiny pearl buttons. In another, she is crying without sound. In another, I am being pulled away by an aunt, or a stranger, or by time itself—algo más fuerte que las manos.

“Mamá,” I said, but my voice stayed inside my mouth.

The station smelled like metal, sweat, old coffee. Men spoke into radios. Women clutched plastic bags full of papers, diapers, sandwiches wrapped in foil. Everywhere, children were being told, “Espérate. Be good. Don’t cry.” Everywhere, we cried.

I did not understand borders then. I only knew doors. Doors that opened. Doors that closed. Doors with guards. Doors behind which my mother disappeared.

For years after, I carried her in pieces: the warm valley of her neck, the red thread bracelet on her wrist, the way she said mi amor as if it were both my name and my shelter. At night, I pressed my face into the pillow and tried to remember her smell before it left me. Soap. Corn masa. Rain on hot pavement. Sometimes I invented it. Sometimes I was afraid I had invented her too.

“What if I never see her again?” I asked no one.

The question became a tiny animal living under my ribs. It scratched when other children ran to their mothers after school. It woke when the phone rang late. It grew teeth when adults whispered in the kitchen, thinking English could hide what Spanish had already told me: papers, court, deportación, money, not yet.

I learned to be a quiet child. Una niña calladita. I folded my longing small enough to fit in my pocket. I smiled in photographs. I ate what was served. I did not ask too often, because asking opened the door, and behind the door was the answer I feared.

But memory, stubborn as a weed, kept bringing her back.

My mother’s hand braiding my hair too tight. My mother blowing on soup. My mother singing while washing dishes, her voice climbing above the clatter—cielito lindo, no llores. Don’t cry. No llores.

I cried anyway.

Years later, when I saw her again, she was smaller than my remembering and larger than my grief. She reached for me, saying my name like she had been holding it in her mouth all that time.

And I understood: separation is not one moment. It is a country you live in. It is learning the shape of absence, the grammar of waiting. It is being a child and discovering that love can be taken from the room, but not from the body.

Even now, when someone leaves, I watch until they turn the corner.

Even now, I whisper, vuelve.

Come back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poetic prose fragment set in La Herradura, El Salvador, narrated by someone recalling their mother leaving, banana groves, planes overhead, and the confusion of remembering reunion years later.
counterfactuals.output:
In La Herradura, the banana groves grew close to the road like a green wall, each leaf torn by wind and sun until it looked like a flag from a country nobody had named. I remember my mother walking beside them with a blue bag in her hand, or perhaps I only remember the story of her walking, told so many times it became a memory with dust on its shoes.

Above us, planes passed over the coast, silver and indifferent, carrying people away or bringing them back. We watched them from the yard, from the shade, from the place where the chickens scratched at the earth. Their sound arrived before their bodies, a trembling in the heat, and I thought the sky itself was opening.

When she left, the afternoon did not change. The sea kept dragging its salt breath through the mangroves. The bananas ripened in their heavy clusters. Someone called my name from inside the house, and I did not answer because I was listening for her steps to return.

Years later, when we met again, I did not know where to put my hands. Her face was both my mother’s and a stranger’s, the way a house can stand in the same place after many storms and still not be the house you entered as a child. She cried. I think I cried too. Or maybe I only remember her tears because they gave me permission to invent my own.

This is how memory confuses mercy with weather: a plane crossing overhead, a grove of bananas shining after rain, a woman leaving, a woman returning, and between them the long, bright distance of La Herradura, where even the dirt road seemed to ask which goodbye had truly happened and which embrace we had imagined in order to survive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental nonfiction monologue that begins “[byline] la herradura, s.v.—” and uses fragmented questions, Spanglish, and sensory memories of a mother to explore abandonment and childhood trauma.
counterfactuals.output:
[byline] la herradura, s.v.—¿y si el abandono tuviera olor? No metaphor, mami. I mean: the real stink of it. Leche agria in a plastic cup. VapoRub under your collarbone. The wet iron smell of rain hitting polvo caliente. Your hair oil—coco, maybe—on the pillowcase after you left for “un ratito,” that little while that stretched its body across my childhood and never stood up.

¿Te acordás? No, of course. Memory is the child’s job. The mother survives by forgetting.

I learned the geography of waiting before I learned the map of El Salvador. La sala. The doorway. The crack under the door where light came in like a lie. The window bars cold against my cheek. The neighbor’s rooster screaming at hours that made no sense. My fingers sticky with mango. My knees scabbed. My mouth full of questions I was told not to ask because “los niños no se meten.”

Where did you go?

Who held your purse?

Did you look back?

Was I sleeping when you decided I was light enough to leave?

I remember your hands most. Not your face. Isn’t that strange? Tus manos: cracked knuckles, uñas cortas, the smell of masa, onion, cheap soap, cigarette smoke you said belonged to someone else. Your palm on my forehead measuring fever like a prophecy. Your thumb wiping dirt from my cheek with spit. Your fingers pinching my arm too hard in public: behave, cállate, don’t embarrass me. Love was pressure. Love was a warning bruise.

And then love was ausencia.

They said you were working. They said you were tired. They said you had to go. They said, “Tu mamá te quiere,” as if wanting could cook dinner, as if wanting could braid my hair, as if wanting could stand between me and the dark hallway where every shadow had a man’s voice.

What is the difference between a mother leaving and a mother being taken by poverty? By fear? By a border? By her own broken girlhood? Tell me so I can stop accusing you in every language I know.

Mami, I have carried you like a hot coin under my tongue. I have spoken around you. I have swallowed you. I have translated you badly: mother = wound, mamá = weather, madre = the first country to expel me.

In La Herradura the air tasted like salt and diesel. The buses coughed black smoke. Vendors sold sliced fruit in plastic bags with limón y chile. Someone was always sweeping dirt from one side of the yard to the other, as if order were possible. The sea was close enough to hear some nights, or maybe that was my stomach. Maybe that was the world leaving and returning, leaving and returning, pretending it was not abandonment but tide.

I was small. That is the whole testimony.

Small enough to believe doors meant return.

Small enough to think if I stayed very quiet, God would notice.

Small enough to confuse hunger with guilt.

When you came back—because sometimes you did, that was the cruelty—you brought sweets. Dulces de leche wrapped in cellophane. A plastic barrette. A dress with stiff lace that scratched my neck. I learned to accept gifts like apologies, to chew sugar over the questions.

¿Me extrañaste?

Did your arms ache?

Did my name rise in your throat and choke you?

Or was I only one more thing you had to put down to keep walking?

Your perfume announced you before your body did. Powdery, floral, too grown for the rooms we lived in. I would smell it and freeze. Joy and terror are twins in a child’s body. I ran to you, then stopped. I wanted to be lifted. I wanted to punish you by not wanting. I wanted to be the kind of daughter who could say no.

But I was open. Always. Like a cut.

At night, other people’s houses made noises: plates, radios, a baby crying, a man laughing too loud, a belt slipped from loops, a dog yelping once and then not again. I learned the inventory of danger through walls. I learned footsteps: drunk, angry, hurried, careful, hers. I learned that a child can leave her body without leaving the room. Float up to the ceiling. Count mosquito bites. Watch herself become furniture.

There are things I won’t name. Not because they didn’t happen. Because naming is another room, and I am tired of rooms.

But I will say this: childhood trauma is not an event. It is a climate. It enters the lungs. It seasons the food. It sits at the table before anyone calls you. It teaches your nervous system to pray with its fists.

Mami, did anyone hold you when you were small? Did your mother leave too? Did she stand in a doorway with the same faraway eyes, already halfway gone? Is abandonment hereditary, like cheekbones, like diabetes, like the way women in our family laugh when they want to die?

I hated you with the devotion of a child. I loved you with the suspicion of an old woman.

Even now, I find you in ordinary things: the burnt edge of a tortilla, the blue flame trembling under a pot, wet laundry slapping against a pila, the metallic taste of fear when someone says they’ll be back soon. I find you in my own hands when they move without permission—folding, cleaning, reaching for a forehead to check for fever. I find you in my flinch. In my tenderness. In the way I pack a bag like escape is a normal season.

You once sang while washing dishes. Do you remember? Your voice low, almost embarrassed. The song broke where the faucet sputtered. I sat under the table, pressing my ear to your ankle. Skin warm. Bone. Soap water dripping onto the floor. For three minutes, I had a mother. Not a story about a mother. Not a rumor. Not a smell left behind in a pillow.

A mother.

Then someone called your name from outside.

Then your body tightened.

Then the song stopped.

I have spent my life inside that silence after the song.

¿Y ahora qué? What do we do with the little girl still waiting by the door? Do we send her back? Do we tell her the truth—that some mothers love from a distance because closeness would expose the ruins? That some mothers leave before they can be left? That some mothers are children wearing adult shoes, walking toward any road that does not ask them to stay?

No. She is too small for theories.

Give her mango. Give her water. Give her a clean sheet. Tell her the night is not her fault. Tell her the footsteps are passing. Tell her she does not have to earn the morning.

Mami, I am not asking anymore why you left.

I am asking what in me is still leaving with you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a short literary passage in the style of a memory collage: a child wonders if they have a mother, remembers lullabies like “arru-rru mi niño,” clothes drying in the sun, dusty sandals, and the belief that their mother will never return.
counterfactuals.output:
Sometimes I wonder if I ever had a mother, or if I invented her from scraps: a song in the dark, *arru-rru mi niño*, the smell of clothes drying stiff in the sun, a blue dress lifting on the line like a small flag of surrender.

There were dusty sandals by the door, always turned toward the road. There was a basin of water gone warm, a comb with black hairs caught in its teeth, the afternoon light lying across the floor as if waiting for someone to step through it.

They said she would come back when the rains came. Then when the corn was high. Then they stopped saying anything at all.

I learned to sleep without listening for footsteps. I learned that some doors remain open only because no one has the heart to close them. Still, at night, the old lullaby rocks inside me, tender and useless, like arms that never return.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a haunting bilingual vignette about migration and maternal absence, told from an older narrator looking back on childhood, mixing present-tense recollection, repeated phrases, and uncertainty about what they truly felt.
counterfactuals.output:
I am old enough now to know that memory is not a house. It has no roof, no floor. It is only a border you keep crossing in the dark.

But in the story I tell myself, I am still eight.

I am standing in the yard with dust on my ankles, watching the road where my mother has disappeared. The road is pale and trembling with heat. The hens scratch at nothing. Somewhere a dog barks as if it has remembered a ghost.

Mi madre se fue al norte.

That is how people say it. Cleanly. As if the north were a room she entered. As if a door closed behind her and not a country, not a river, not a thousand miles of men asking questions.

She went north.  
She went north.  
Mi madre se fue.

I do not remember crying. Or I remember crying because everyone tells me I cried. My aunt says I clung to my mother’s skirt until she peeled my fingers away one by one. My brother says I stood very straight, como soldadito, like a little soldier, and would not look at anyone. In my own memory, I am neither brave nor broken. I am simply there, looking at the road, holding a mango pit in my mouth, tasting sweetness and rot.

Maybe I felt nothing.

Maybe nothing was the feeling.

At night, my grandmother lays me beside her and says, “Tu mamá va a volver.” Your mother will come back. She says it into my hair, into the dark, into the place where my mother’s breathing used to be. I listen to the insects tapping at the walls. I listen for footsteps. I listen so hard that the whole world becomes footsteps.

Va a volver.  
Va a volver.  
She will come back.

In the mornings, I wake and find she has not.

This is childhood: a cup of coffee gone cold on the table, a dress hanging from a nail, the smell of jabón and smoke, the shadow of a woman moving through rooms where no woman moves. This is migration: a mother becoming a voice, then a photograph, then money folded into envelopes, then a story told by adults when they think the children are asleep.

“She’s doing it for you,” they say.

Por ti.  
For you.

I did not know what to do with that kind of love. It was too large to hold and too far away to touch. It bought shoes. It paid school fees. It crossed deserts. It did not braid my hair.

Sometimes the phone rings at the corner store, and we run. We run as if the ringing is a body returning. My grandmother wipes her hands on her apron. My brother arrives barefoot. I stand beneath the counter, listening to the wire carry my mother’s breath.

“Mija,” she says.

Her voice is thin, full of weather.

I want to ask: Did you eat? Are you cold? Do you sleep with the light on? Do you miss me or only remember me? But I am a child, and children are trained to answer.

“Estoy bien,” I say. I am fine.

I am fine.  
Estoy bien.  
I am fine.

Maybe I was.

After the call, everyone says how lucky we are. We have a mother in el norte. We have hope with an address. We have dollars coming like pale birds from another sky.

But that night I dream her hands are knocking from inside the walls.

Years pass. Or they do not pass; they gather. I grow into the space she left, which is not the same as healing. I learn to cook rice without burning it. I learn which saints receive which candles. I learn that a passport can be a miracle and a wound. I learn to pronounce absence in two languages.

Mother.  
Madre.  
Mamá.

Each word opens a different door. Behind each door, she is leaving.

When she finally returns, I am taller than she remembers. She touches my face with both hands, as if searching for the child she left there. I smell perfume, airplane, soap from a country I have never seen. Her hair is shorter. Mine is unbraided.

We stand in the doorway.

No one tells you that reunion can look like strangers being polite.

She says, “Mi niña.”

I think I say, “Mamá.”

I think I go to her. I think I let her hold me. Or perhaps I stiffen. Perhaps I forgive her immediately. Perhaps I never do. Memory lowers its eyes.

All I know is this: for years after, whenever she walked to the market, to church, to the next room, I watched her back until it vanished. I watched the road. I watched the door.

Even now, old as I am, I wake before dawn and listen.

I listen for footsteps.  
Escucho pasos.  
I listen for the mother leaving, the mother returning, the mother who is always somewhere between here and there.

And still I cannot say what I felt.

Only that the road was pale.  
Only that the hens scratched at nothing.  
Only that my mouth held the taste of mango, sweetness and rot.

Only that she went north.

Mi madre se fue al norte.

And part of me is standing there still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
